```{r}
#| label: reweight
# Joint reweighting: every weight multiplied by its own factor between one half
# and two (2^u, u uniform on [-1, 1]), the score recomputed from the item
# scores of the live report. The distribution is a convention of this report.
pkgload::load_all(pkg_dir, quiet = TRUE, export_all = FALSE, helpers = FALSE)
item_table <- function(f) {
  r <- tf_check(tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", f)))
  w <- vapply(r$items, function(i) i$weight, numeric(1))
  s <- vapply(r$items, function(i) if (is.null(i$score)) NA_real_ else i$score,
              numeric(1))
  list(w = w, s = s, score = r$aggregate_score, range = r$aggregate_range,
       ids = vapply(r$items, function(i) i$id, character(1)))
}
blk <- tf_check(tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", adv[1])))$items
n_blockers <- sum(vapply(blk, function(i) identical(i$severity_if_fail, "blocker"), logical(1)))
rw_files <- c(adv, strong_all)
items <- lapply(rw_files, item_table)
names(items) <- rw_files
n_items <- length(items[[1]]$w)
set.seed(20261125)
n_draw <- 4000
fac <- matrix(2^runif(n_draw * n_items, -1, 1), ncol = n_items)
rw <- sapply(items, function(it) {
  ok <- !is.na(it$s)
  stopifnot(round(100 * sum(it$w[ok] * it$s[ok]) / sum(it$w[ok]), 1) == it$score)
  as.vector(100 * (fac[, ok, drop = FALSE] %*% (it$w[ok] * it$s[ok])) /
              (fac[, ok, drop = FALSE] %*% it$w[ok]))
})
p_adv_over_enc <- mean(apply(rw[, adv, drop = FALSE], 1, min) >
                         apply(rw[, strong_enc, drop = FALSE], 1, max))
p_adv_over_consc <- mean(apply(rw[, adv, drop = FALSE], 1, min) >
                           apply(rw[, consc, drop = FALSE], 1, max))
outside <- sapply(rw_files, function(f) {
  r <- items[[f]]$range
  mean(rw[, f] < r[1] - 0.05 | rw[, f] > r[2] + 0.05)
})
width_ratio <- sapply(rw_files, function(f) {
  q <- quantile(rw[, f], c((1 - ci_level) / 2, 1 - (1 - ci_level) / 2))
  r <- items[[f]]$range
  if (diff(r) == 0) NA else unname(diff(q) / diff(r))
})
rt1 <- "adversarial/rt1-tautology.theory.yaml"
s1c <- "strong/s1-light-deflection-conscientious.theory.yaml"
p_rt1_over_s1c <- mean(rw[, rt1] > rw[, s1c])
# A file that passes every item that applies to it scores 100 under any
# positive weights, and a file with an applicable item below 1 scores less.
all_pass <- function(f) all(items[[f]]$s[!is.na(items[[f]]$s)] == 1)
full_adv <- adv[vapply(adv, all_pass, logical(1))]
strong_below <- all(!vapply(strong_all, all_pass, logical(1)))
```

```{r}
#| label: summary-numbers
# Agreement of the pilot encoders' independence models over the constructs all
# three used, needed in the summary: the share of statements on which all
# three agreed and Fleiss' kappa, which no interval accompanies.
indep <- rd("pilot/independence_model_common.csv")
th_lab <- c("bilingual-rhm" = "RHM", "collaborative-cognitive-load" = "CCLT",
            "health-habit" = "habit")
im <- indep[match(names(th_lab), indep$theory), ]
hb <- im[im$theory == "health-habit", ]
two <- im[im$theory != "health-habit", ]
hb_share <- unlist(hb[, paste0("share_independent_enc-", 1:3)])
kappa_text <- if (nrow(two) == 2 && nrow(hb) == 1 &&
                  hb$all_three_agree < min(two$all_three_agree)) {
  paste0("All three encoders agreed on ", pcts(two$all_three_agree),
         " of the statements for two theories (Fleiss' kappa ",
         and_list(num(two$fleiss_kappa, 2)), ") and on ",
         pct(hb$all_three_agree), " for the third, whose source leaves open ",
         "whether habit prompts repetition directly or through behaviour. That ",
         "choice decides whether many of the statements are independences, and ",
         "kappa for that theory, ", num(hb$fleiss_kappa, 2), ", is unstable, since ",
         "the three encodings state an independence for ",
         pcts(hb_share, 1), " of the statements.")
} else {
  paste0("All three encoders agreed on ", pcts(im$all_three_agree),
         " of the statements for the three theories (Fleiss' kappa ",
         and_list(num(im$fleiss_kappa, 2)), ").")
}
# The verdicts of sound with caveats kept unchanged whose caveat no document
# states.
r_lisrel <- vrow("Compiled syntax fits with lavaan::sem() as written (one feedback loop)")
stopifnot(grepl("LISREL representation refuses", r_lisrel$note, fixed = TRUE))
undoc_text <- if (length(undoc_ids) == 0) "" else paste0(
  " For ", nw(length(undoc_ids)), ", ", and_list(undoc_ids), ", the caveat is ",
  "still undocumented",
  if (identical(undoc_ids, "statistics-and-simulation-v16")) paste0(
    ": lavaan's default representation refuses ", nw(r_lisrel$discrepancies),
    " of the ", int(r_lisrel$cases), " compiled models with a feedback loop ",
    "that the auditors fitted, and no document says so") else "",
  ".")
```

# Summary {.unnumbered}

The maintainer of theoryforge asked whether its R and Python packages and the
two browser apps that run them are trustworthy and scientifically valid, and
doubted that appraising scientific theories, a matter of human judgement for
decades, can be done automatically. This report draws on an audit of the code at
commit f72ce4c by `r nw(n_lens)` auditors, each examining the package from one
point of view (a lens) and each rechecked by an independent second reader, on an
encoding pilot and on reruns of the same evidence on version `r pkg_version`.
Every auditor, second reader and encoder was an AI agent, as was the drafter of
this report and of its status register, written for the maintainer. No human
expert took part. That limits what the evidence can show, and the limits are set
out in @sec-limits.

The answer differs by component. The package's deductions from a stated causal
graph, its implied conditional independencies, the signs of effects and
associations, its adjustment sets and its equivalence classes, can be trusted as
deduction. Its numerical routines, post-data severity, the compilation of
structural equation models and the exact simulation, compute what they are
specified to compute. In `r int(vk("package"))` checks, an output of the package
was compared with independent software, the auditors' own implementations of
the definitions or analytic and published values (@sec-core). The package
agreed in every case in `r int(vk("package", "clean"))` of them,
`r int(vk("package", "size"))` measured a rate, a coverage or the size of an
approximation, and each of the `r int(vk("package", "disc"))` that found a
discrepancy lies outside an assumption the documentation states, concerns the
wording of a document or was graded minor. The R and Python twins gave the same
results in all `r int(vk("parity"))` comparisons of their outputs, and
`r int(vk("other"))` further checks examined sentences of the documentation,
design arguments and a reference implementation.

The deductions hold under assumptions the package cannot check. The graph must
be the causal structure among the constructs, and every pair of constructs that
no proposition joins is read as having no direct effect and no unexplained
association, so the deductions are commitments of the theory only if its
authors meant those omissions. Each relation must act in its stated direction
whatever the other inputs, as in a linear or uniformly monotone model, some
verdicts assume faithfulness, and a construct marked latent is read as if it
were measured. For feedback loops read by sigma-separation, each loop must
settle to a unique equilibrium, the system must be stable with the intervened
construct held fixed for the signs of effects and as observed for the signs of
associations, and a conditional association called 'nonzero' assumes a
nonlinear model. The numerical routines carry conditions of their own.
Post-data severity treats the standard error as known and as describing the
sampling distribution at the bound, and it takes no account of selection. A
simulation run is one linear system consistent with the stated signs, with gains
and damping that the theory does not state. A compiled model fixes at zero the
covariances the theory omits, so a small omitted correlation can make the global
fit reject a model whose propositions are all true. Every output, finally,
describes the file and not the theory. In the pilot, the independence models
that encoders of the same short text produced were compared over the constructs
all three used. `r kappa_text`

The checklist score cannot be trusted to mean what its earlier name, a rigour
score, suggested. It describes how completely a file fills in what the checklist
asks for. In the live run of version `r pkg_version`, as at f72ce4c, files that
are empty of content, circular or refuted by every recorded test pass the gate
and score above every established theory as first encoded from its source, and
`r nw(n_adv_above_consc)` of the `r nw(n_adv)` score above every one of those
theories re-encoded with all the fields their sources allow. The amendment
appraisal applies fixed rules to what two versions of a file declare. It cannot
tell a prediction from an accommodation and does not weigh how good a test was.
Its verdicts have not been compared with any expert's.

Of the `r int(n_find)` findings in the register, version `r pkg_version` fixed
`r int(nf("fixed"))` and now reports `r int(nf("reported"))` beside a verdict or
gate that it leaves unchanged. For the `r nw(n_rep_loop)` reported findings on
feedback loops, the derivation chain now warns about a claim that a loop
leaves unread and names it, while the score counts the claim as derived and
the gate still passes. The release answered
`r int(nf("reworded"))` findings by rewording what the outputs and documents
say, with the behaviour unchanged, and left `r int(nf(not_changed))` unchanged,
`r int(nf("deferred"))` of them for expansions the maintainer plans for version
0.9.0 but has not published. Of the `r int(n_verd)` verdicts on components and
claims, the status register counts `r status_phrase(vd$status)`. Not applicable
marks verdicts of sound that needed no change. The reworded verdicts include
`r int(n_rw_rework)` whose recommendation was to rework the component. The
unchanged ones include `r int(n_caveat_unch)` verdicts of sound with caveats
whose recommendation was to keep. For `r nw(sum(cav_doc))` of them, the
documentation already stated the caveat, and for `r nw(sum(cav_src))`, the
caveat concerns the auditors' own reading of a source.`r undoc_text`

The main behavioural corrections concern two rules. The amendment appraisal now
reads the signs the two graphs entail, so an amendment that reverses a
corroborated prediction is no longer called progressive, and it withholds
that verdict when the graph of either version cannot be built. The checklist's
derivation chain now reads, under the default, every claim that no feedback
loop reaches, so a loop elsewhere in the graph no longer lets a contradicted
claim through the gate. A claim that names a construct on a loop or downstream
of one is still not read: the item warns and names it but counts it as derived,
and the claim cannot block the gate. The score still rates empty, circular and
refuted files highly. Apart from the derivation chain and a few narrower rules,
the release changed what the score is called and what is said about it, not
what it computes. A review of the release found problems in the corrected rules, and a
second round of corrections addressed them before this report (@sec-changes).
That round changed how the deductive core reads a graph with a loop, and the
change was checked against independent oracles (@sec-loops).

This evidence answers in part whether automated appraisal of theories is
feasible. Deduction from a stated graph can be automated soundly, and a fixed
rule can describe how complete a file is and apply declared outcomes
consistently. No part of the package has shown that it can judge a theory's
quality, truth or fruitfulness, or tell a prediction from an accommodation, and
no study yet links its outputs to human judgement. The protocol in this folder
(`protocol.qmd`) describes `r nw(n_studies)` studies with human participants
that would measure what the audit could not, with expert judgement, itself
fallible, as the criterion for the checklist and the appraisal.

# How the audit was done {#sec-method}

## Lenses, second readers and the pilot

The audit examined the code and documentation at commit f72ce4c, whose code is
the same as that of b5ebf84, the release candidate before the corrections
described in @sec-changes. It was organised by lens, each lens being one auditor
that examined the package from one point of view. `r Nw(n_formal)` formal lenses
examined the claims the package and its documents make (the claims register),
the causal deductions, the statistics and the simulation, and the checklist
score, tested by files built to score highly without content (a red team).
`r Nw(n_conceptual)` conceptual lenses examined the package from the philosophy
of science, from measurement theory, from metascience and the related tools, and
from the communication of results in the documents and apps. Each lens wrote its
own scripts, ran them on a detached checkout of the commit and reported verdicts
on components and graded findings.

An independent second reader then rechecked each lens. The second reader reran
the lens's scripts on a fresh checkout, compared the outputs and rechecked the
references. It upheld, regraded or withdrew the findings it checked, changed
verdicts where the evidence called for it and added defects the lens had missed.
The register in `data/` keeps both readings, and where they differ, this report
follows the second reader.

In a pilot, `r nw(length(unique(rd("pilot/checklist_by_encoder.csv")$encoder)))`
encoders each encoded the same
`r nw(length(unique(rd("pilot/checklist_by_encoder.csv")$theory)))` verbal
theories into theory files: the Revised Hierarchical Model of bilingual memory
[@kroll2010], collaborative cognitive load theory [@kirschner2018] and an
account of habit in health behaviour [@gardner2015]. Each encoder worked from a
summary of `r int(min(src_words))` to `r int(max(src_words))` words that one
agent wrote from the published sources, and one agent, as analyst, matched
constructs and coded the statements. The pilot had no second reader.

## Rules of evidence and grading

The auditors followed written rules. Every claim had to rest on something a
reader can check: a script and its output, a line of the code or documentation
at the audited commit, or a published source verified against Crossref or PubMed
for authors, year, title, journal or book, volume, issue, pages and DOI.
Positions were not to be attributed to authors from memory. The register lists
`r int(nrow(refs))` verified references. Some texts could not be read, because
they are behind paywalls or because the network refused their hosts. Where a
verdict depends on what such a source holds, the register says that it rests on
the auditor's reasoning instead.

Each component or claim received one verdict: sound (correct and adequately
justified), sound with caveats (correct under assumptions the documentation
should state), questionable (weakly or contestably justified), unsupported (no
evidence that it measures or shows what it says) or wrong (demonstrably
incorrect), with a recommendation to keep, qualify, rework, remove or extend.
Each finding was graded critical (users would draw wrong scientific
conclusions), major or minor.

## Who did the audit

Every lens, every second reader and every pilot encoder was an AI agent, an
instance of a Claude model working from written instructions, and so were the
writer of the pilot's source summaries and its analyst. No human expert took
part. The maintainer commissioned the work and reads this report. An AI agent of
the same family drafted the report and the status register of @sec-status. This
bounds what the audit can show. The agents share training and are likely to
share blind spots, so a second reader is independent of a lens in the sense that
it reran the evidence, not in the sense that a second human expert would be. The
pilot's encoders are not researchers in the domains they encoded, read the same
documentation and may have made the same choices for the same reasons. And no
human judgement of theory quality was available to compare the package's outputs
with, so every statement in this report about misreading or about agreement with
experts is a judgement of the auditors and has not been measured.

## What the audit found

The register holds `r int(n_find)` findings: `r int(n_find_lens)` raised by the
lenses and the pilot (`r int(n_find_pilot)` of them by the pilot) and
`r int(n_find_reader)` that the second readers said the lenses had missed. The
second readers rechecked `r int(n_lens_checked)` of the `r int(n_lens_np)`
findings the lenses raised. The other
`r int(n_lens_np - n_lens_checked)`, all graded `r and_list(unchecked_sev)` by
their lens, were not rechecked. Of those rechecked, the readers upheld
`r int(n_upheld)`, some at another grade. In all, they lowered the grade of
`r int(n_down)`, raised `r nw(n_up)` and withdrew `r nw(n_withdrawn)`. They
marked `r nw(n_notup)` further findings as not upheld without withdrawing them
and kept them as narrower or lesser defects, `r nw(n_notup_lowered)` of them
lowered from major to minor. Of the `r int(n_find_reader)` defects the second
readers added, `r int(n_reader_ungraded)` carry no grade, and no one rechecked
them. @tbl-findings counts the findings by lens and severity, with the ungraded
ones under 'Other', so the counts of critical and major findings leave them out.
The `r nw(n_crit)` critical findings concern the amendment appraisal, what the
checklist score measures and how it is presented, and the effect of feedback
loops on the derivation check. They are listed with their status in
@tbl-critical.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-findings
#| tbl-cap: "Findings by lens and severity (the second reader's grade where there is one). 'Other' counts the finding the second reader withdrew and the defects added without a grade."
sev_tab <- function(rows) {
  c(Critical = sum(rows$sev == "critical"), Major = sum(rows$sev == "major"),
    Minor = sum(rows$sev == "minor"),
    Other = sum(rows$sev %in% c("none", "ungraded")), Total = nrow(rows))
}
t1 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lens_short), function(l) sev_tab(fd[fd$lens == l, ])))
t1 <- rbind(t1, sev_tab(fd))
t1 <- data.frame(Lens = c(unname(lens_short), "All"), t1, check.names = FALSE)
kab(t1)
```

```{r}
#| label: verdict-pattern
# Verdicts of questionable, unsupported or wrong on the deductive core against
# those on the checklist, the appraisal and their presentation.
against <- vd$v %in% c("questionable", "unsupported", "wrong")
core_groups <- c("Deductive core", "Post-data severity and test plans",
                 "SEM compilation", "Simulation")
judged_groups <- c("Checklist and score", "Amendment appraisal",
                   "Fixed rules as appraisal", "Documents and framing", "Apps")
n_against <- sum(against)
n_against_judged <- sum(against & vd$group %in% judged_groups)
core_ok <- sum(vd$group %in% core_groups & vd$v %in% c("sound", "sound with caveats"))
core_n <- sum(vd$group %in% core_groups)
```

The `r int(n_verd)` verdicts cover components and claims across the packages,
the documents and the apps. The second readers checked `r int(n_verd_checked)`
of them and changed `r int(n_verd_changed)`. @tbl-verdicts groups them by the
component they concern. Of the `r int(core_n)` verdicts on the deductive and
numerical core, `r int(core_ok)` are sound or sound with caveats, while
`r int(n_against_judged)` of the `r int(n_against)` verdicts of questionable,
unsupported or wrong concern the checklist, the appraisal and the way the
documents and apps present them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-verdicts
#| tbl-cap: "Verdicts by component (the second reader's verdict where it changed). 'Caveats' is sound with caveats. 'Against' is unsupported or wrong."
vt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(group_order, function(g) {
  r <- vd[vd$group == g, ]
  data.frame(Component = g, Sound = sum(r$v == "sound"),
             Caveats = sum(r$v == "sound with caveats"),
             Questionable = sum(r$v == "questionable"),
             Against = sum(r$v %in% c("unsupported", "wrong")), Total = nrow(r))
}))
vt <- rbind(vt, data.frame(Component = "All", Sound = sum(vd$v == "sound"),
                           Caveats = sum(vd$v == "sound with caveats"),
                           Questionable = sum(vd$v == "questionable"),
                           Against = sum(vd$v %in% c("unsupported", "wrong")),
                           Total = nrow(vd)))
kab(vt)
```

## Status in version `r pkg_version` {#sec-status}

For each finding and verdict, `data/status-0.8.0.csv` records what version
`r pkg_version` does about it, with the file or rerun that shows it. Fixed means
that the behaviour or rule was corrected. Reported means that the package now
reports the problem beside its result without changing the verdict or the gate
that the finding concerns. For the `r nw(n_rep_loop)` reported findings on
feedback loops, the derivation chain now warns and names the claims it could
not read, while the score counts them as derived and the gate still passes.
Reworded means that the outputs and documentation now say
what is computed while the behaviour is unchanged. Unchanged means that nothing
was done. Deferred marks a
finding left unchanged whose remedy is one of the expansions the maintainer
plans for version 0.9.0, data tests of implications, ensemble simulation,
interoperability and a teaching mode. The register records that plan in its
verdicts on planned features, but no document publishes it, so a deferred
finding is best read as unchanged. Remedies that the audit recommended for a
later release and that the plan does not include count as unchanged. Withdrawn
marks the finding the second reader withdrew, and not applicable marks verdicts
of sound whose recommendation was to keep the component as it is. A verdict of
sound with caveats whose recommendation was to keep counts as reworded where
version `r pkg_version` states its caveat in more places than before, and
otherwise as unchanged, whether the documentation already stated the caveat, the
caveat concerns the auditors' own reading of a source or no document states it.
Other verdicts are classed as findings are, by what was done.

A finding is classed by the part of it that the second reader stated, and where
part of what its title names remains, the basis says so. The status was
established by rerunning the audit's evidence against the code of this
repository where a script exists, as `r int(n_basis_rerun)` of the
`r int(nrow(st))` bases record, and otherwise by reading the files at this
commit, never from commit messages alone. AI agents assigned the status of each
row, and the column `checked` records which rows were checked again. The agents
that drafted and revised this report rechecked `r int(n_chk_drafter)` rows, and
reviewers of the draft, also AI agents, reran the evidence or reread the files
for `r int(n_chk_reviewer)`, `r int(n_chk_both)` of them in both checks. Of the
`r int(n_chk)` rows checked, `r int(n_chk_status)` now carry a different status
from the one the classifying agent gave them, because a check found them
misclassified or because the definitions of the statuses were narrowed, and
`r int(n_chk_basis)` kept their status with a qualified basis, as the column
`revised` records. The other `r int(n_unchk)` rows rest on the classifying
agent's reading alone, though `r int(n_unchk_status)` of them changed status
when the definitions were narrowed. The classifying agents did not record which
rows they were unsure of.

After a review of the release, a second round of corrections changed the code
again. The evidence of the `r int(n_r2)` rows whose status or basis that round
changed was rerun on the final code, as the column `second_round` records:
`r r2_status_phrase` and `r int(n_r2_basis)` kept their status with a new basis.
Of these rows, `r int(n_r2_unchk)` are among those that no one had checked
before, so their bases now rest on that rerun. The counts in this report are
read from the file, so they follow it.

# The deductive core {#sec-core}

```{r}
#| label: core-numbers
r_basis <- vrow("Basis statements on acyclic graphs are d-separations")
r_min <- vrow("Minimal statements on acyclic graphs are d-separations")
r_sig <- vrow("Basis statements under cycles = 'sigma' are sigma-separations")
r_sig_cyc <- vrow("Sigma statements on cyclic graphs are also d-separations")
r_sig_lin <- vrow("Sigma statements on cyclic graphs hold in linear models")
r_insep <- vrow("Inseparable pairs on acyclic graphs have no separating set")
r_dense <- vrow("Basis statements on 160 dense acyclic graphs")
r_reader <- vrow("Basis statements on the second reader's random theories")
r_parity <- vrow("Entailment, implication and equivalence records under refuse and sigma")
r_latent <- vrow("Testable independencies among observed constructs when some constructs are latent")
r_comp <- vrow("Documented sentence that every other independence follows")
r_eff <- vrow("Effect signs on acyclic graphs (effect claims)")
eff_signed <- note_num(r_eff, "Positive \\(([0-9,]+)\\)") +
  note_num(r_eff, "negative \\(([0-9,]+)\\)")
eff_zero <- note_num(r_eff, "zero \\(([0-9,]+)\\)")
eff_open <- note_num(r_eff, "all ([0-9,]+) 'undetermined'")
stopifnot(eff_signed + eff_zero + eff_open == r_eff$cases)
r_ass <- vrow("Marginal association signs on acyclic graphs")
r_cond <- vrow("Conditional associations on acyclic graphs")
r_nonlin <- vrow("Effect and association signs on acyclic graphs in monotone nonlinear models")
r_regA <- vrow("Effect signs under cycles = 'sigma', regime A")
r_regB <- vrow("Signed effects under cycles = 'sigma', regime B")
r_stab <- vrow("Effect signs under cycles = 'sigma' when the system with x held fixed is stable")
r_unstab <- vrow("Effect signs under cycles = 'sigma' when the system with x held fixed is unstable")
r_sig_nz <- vrow("Conditional 'nonzero' under cycles = 'sigma', regime A")
r_vwr <- vrow("Signed marginal associations against VanderWeele and Robins")
r_rules <- vrow("Claim verdicts and faithfulness flags recomputed")
r_adj <- vrow("'identified' (covariate adjustment) agrees with dagitty::adjustmentSets() (effect claims)")
r_id <- vrow("'identified' (covariate adjustment) against identifiability by the ID algorithm")
r_lat_x <- vrow("'identified' for effects of a latent exposure")
r_eq <- vrow("Compelled edges equal dagitty::equivalenceClass()")
r_eq_cl <- vrow("Compelled edges equal causal-learn's dag2cpdag")
r_dir <- vrow("Documented claim that no observational study can tell a reversible direction apart")
r_spanos <- vrow("One-bound severity against a published table")
r_spanos_r <- vrow("Residual against Spanos (2024), Table 1")
spanos_tol <- note_num(r_spanos, "within ([0-9]*\\.[0-9]+)")
spanos_tol_r <- note_num(r_spanos_r, "within ([0-9]*\\.[0-9]+)")
r_toster <- vrow("Two-bound severity equals 1 minus the TOSTmeta() p value")
r_sevpar <- vrow("post_data_severity() (random one- and two-bound cases)")
r_sem_id <- vrow("Compiled model is locally identified")
r_sem_eq <- vrow("Compiled model equals the theory's model written in full (acyclic)")
r_sem_eff <- vrow("Defined effects equal the total effect")
r_bow <- vrow("Bow comment: the path is not identified")
r_semparity <- vrow("compile_sem() syntax (random theories)")
r_expm <- vrow("Exact method against the matrix exponential propagated step by step (runs)")
r_ode <- vrow("Exact method against an ODE solver (runs)")
r_lsoda <- vrow("Exact method (R) against an ODE solver (runs)")
r_simpar <- vrow("simulate() trajectories, exact and Euler (runs)")
r_euler <- vrow("Euler departure warning against the documented rule (runs)")
ode_text <- if (r_ode$cases == r_lsoda$cases) {
  paste(int(r_ode$cases), "runs of each solver")
} else paste(int(r_ode$cases), "and", int(r_lsoda$cases), "runs")
```

The deductive core is the part of the package that derives consequences from the
causal graph that a file's propositions state, and the numerical functions built
on it. The causal-verification and statistics lenses and their second readers
compared it with independent implementations on random theories and with
published values. @tbl-verification summarises the `r int(n_checks)` checks in
`data/verification.csv`. Of these, `r int(vk("package"))` compare an output of
the package with independent software, the auditors' own implementation of a
definition or an analytic or published value, and they are counted by
component. The `r int(vk("parity"))` comparisons of the R and Python twins and
the `r int(vk("other"))` checks of sentences of the documentation, of design
arguments, of a reference implementation and of the package against itself are
counted apart. @tbl-discrepancies in the appendix lists every check that found a
discrepancy. The `r int(n_rerun)` checks whose notes end 'Rerun on 0.8.0: same
result.' were rerun on version `r pkg_version` and gave the audit's numbers. The
R and Python engines gave identical causal records on the
`r int(r_parity$cases)` random theories of the causal verification, and the
status register records the same for a rerun at `r pkg_version`. These checks
describe the audited code. The final `r pkg_version` reads a graph with a
feedback loop differently, and that change was checked separately
(@sec-loops).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-verification
#| tbl-cap: "Checks of the deductive and numerical core. A check measures one quantity against one comparator. The rows by component count comparisons of the package's output with an independent implementation or value. 'Size only' counts checks that measure a rate, a coverage or the size of an approximation rather than agreement."
vt_row <- function(label, r) {
  data.frame(Component = label, Checks = nrow(r),
             Agree = sum(!is.na(r$discrepancies) & r$discrepancies == 0),
             Differ = sum(!is.na(r$discrepancies) & r$discrepancies > 0),
             "Size only" = sum(is.na(r$discrepancies)), check.names = FALSE)
}
pk <- ver[ver$kind == "package", ]
vt2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(pk$component), function(cmp) {
  vt_row(cap(cmp), pk[pk$component == cmp, ])
}))
vt2 <- rbind(vt2, vt_row("R and Python twins", ver[ver$kind == "parity", ]),
             vt_row("Documentation, design and comparators", ver[ver$kind == "other", ]))
vt2 <- rbind(vt2, data.frame(Component = "All", Checks = sum(vt2$Checks),
                             Agree = sum(vt2$Agree), Differ = sum(vt2$Differ),
                             "Size only" = sum(vt2[["Size only"]]),
                             check.names = FALSE))
kab(vt2)
```

## Implied independencies

On acyclic graphs, every one of the `r int(r_basis$cases)` basis statements and
`r int(r_min$cases)` minimal statements that `implications()` gave for the
random theories was a d-separation according to networkx, dagitty and a search
written from the definition, and every pair the package called inseparable
(`r int(r_insep$cases)`) had no separating set. The same held on dense graphs
(`r int(r_dense$cases)` statements) and on the second reader's own generator
(`r int(r_reader$cases)` statements). Under `cycles = "sigma"`, all
`r int(r_sig$cases)` basis statements were sigma-separations according to a
search written from the definition. Only the `r int(r_sig_cyc$cases)` of them on
graphs with feedback loops test the sigma reading, since on an acyclic graph it
equals d-separation. In exact linear models, every statement had a partial
covariance of zero, on graphs with loops when the spectral radius of the
absolute coefficient matrix was below one (`r int(r_sig_lin$cases)`
statements).

Some qualifications remain. The sentence that every other independence follows
from the basis set needs the distribution to have the composition property, as a
multivariate normal one does. A discrete counterexample breaks it, and the
documents now say so. A construct marked latent is read like any other, so for
`r int(r_latent$discrepancies)` of the `r int(r_latent$cases)` pairs that
dagitty can test among observed constructs, the package's statement holds a
latent construct fixed and no observed alternative is sought. The help now says
this. Projecting latent constructs out was left for a later release, for which
no plan is published. Most important for users, every pair of constructs that no
proposition joins becomes an implied independence. The statements are
commitments of the theory only if its authors meant those omissions, which the
help and the preregistration now say.

## Sign entailments and their assumptions

On acyclic graphs in linear models, the derived verdicts held for all
`r int(r_eff$cases)` effect claims, `r int(r_ass$cases)` marginal associations
and `r int(r_cond$cases)` conditional associations. Of the effect claims,
`r int(eff_signed)` were derived as positive or negative and `r int(eff_zero)`
as zero, and the `r int(eff_open)` left undetermined took both signs. In random
monotone nonlinear models, the verdicts held for `r int(r_nonlin$cases)`
model-claims, where 'positive' then means non-negative. The second reader
recomputed the verdict and faithfulness rules for `r int(r_rules$cases)` claims
with every claimed sign and found no mismatch, and checked `r int(r_vwr$cases)`
signed associations against the published sufficient condition of VanderWeele
and Robins [-@vanderweele2010].

Feedback loops need more. Under sigma-separation with the spectral radius of the
absolute coefficient matrix below one, the `r int(r_regA$cases)` effect claims
held. Where the system was stable but that radius was not below one,
`r int(r_regB$discrepancies)` of `r int(r_regB$cases)` signed effects failed.
The second reader located the failures: in `r int(r_stab$cases)` random draws in
which the system with the intervened construct held fixed is stable, no sign
failed, while `r int(r_unstab$discrepancies)` of the `r int(r_unstab$cases)`
draws in which it is unstable failed. So the signs on cyclic graphs hold when
the system after the intervention settles, a condition the documentation at
f72ce4c left ambiguous and the help, the specification and the apps now state.

The signs therefore rest on assumptions the package cannot check: that the graph
is the causal structure among the constructs, that each signed relation acts in
its direction whatever the other inputs, which a moderator that reverses an
effect breaks, that errors are independent apart from the stated associations
and, for loops, stability with the intervened construct held fixed for effects
and of the system as observed for associations. Some
verdicts rest on faithfulness as well, with two consequences. A conditional
association called 'nonzero' under sigma-separation can be zero in every linear
cyclic model with the graph, as `r int(r_sig_nz$discrepancies)` of
`r int(r_sig_nz$cases)` such claims were. And a claimed zero effect through two
paths of opposite sign is reported as contradicted, although the graph leaves
its value open. The claim line now adds 'unless effects cancel exactly', and the
derivation check still fails it.

## Adjustment sets and what 'identified' means

Whether adjusting for some set of the theory's constructs identifies an effect
agreed with dagitty in all `r int(r_adj$cases)` effect claims, and every set
returned was one of dagitty's minimal sets. 'Identified' means that adjusting
for some of the theory's constructs identifies the effect, and a value of false
does not mean that the effect cannot be identified. Of `r int(r_id$cases)`
claims checked against the ID algorithm, the package said 'not identified' for
`r int(r_id$discrepancies)` that the algorithm identifies. Almost all are
effects that are zero because the exposure does not cause the outcome, and
identifying those assumes the very claim a test would examine. No claim was
identified by adjustment and not by the algorithm. The package also reports an
adjustment set for an exposure marked latent, as it did for
`r int(r_lat_x$discrepancies)` of `r int(r_lat_x$cases)` such effects, though an
unmeasured exposure cannot be adjusted for in a test. The help and the
specification now say what 'identified' means and what a latent exposure
assumes. The preregistration still prints the set without that caveat.

## Claims beside feedback loops {#sec-loops}

After the audit, version `r pkg_version` changed how the core reads a graph
with a feedback loop. Under the default, `cycles = "refuse"`, a claim that names
a construct on a loop or downstream of one is left unread, and any other claim
gets the record it would get on the graph without the loop, its adjustment set
included. AI agents checked the change against oracles that do not use
theoryforge (`data/loop-verification.csv`). In `r int(lv_theories)` random
theories with loops, the package left unread exactly those of the
`r int(lv_gate$claims)` claims that the verifiers' own reachability placed
behind a loop. Each of the `r int(lv_sigma$claims)` claims it read got, in every
field, the record that sigma-separation gives and the record that the code
before the change gives on the acyclic graph of the claim's ancestors, and
their signs and verdicts held in sampled linear models of the full graph with
stable loops. The R and Python twins gave the same `r int(lv_twin$claims)` claim
records. `r lv_text`
once `r nw(lv_flagged)` claims with a draw near zero were redrawn with
well-conditioned coefficients. The linear-model checks ran on commit
`r and_list(lv_old)`, which gives the same verdicts as the final code. The
oracles implement the definitions as their authors, also AI agents, read them,
on random graphs of up to `r int(lv_kmax)` constructs.

## Equivalence classes

The compelled and reversible edges equalled those of dagitty, ggm and
causal-learn in all `r int(r_eq$cases)` acyclic theories without associations
(those of two or more constructs). The class is right for
tests of conditional independence. The documents at f72ce4c said that no
observational study could tell a reversible direction apart, which is wrong as
worded: in a demonstration with non-Gaussian errors, a test of residual
dependence chose the true direction. Version `r pkg_version` says instead that
no test of conditional independence can settle the direction, which needs an
intervention, a temporal order or distributional assumptions.
`equivalent_models()` cannot know which constructs a study manipulates, so a
direction fixed by experiment can still be listed as reversible.

## Post-data severity

`post_data_severity()` reproduced the published one-sided values the audit
compared it with, all `r nw(r_spanos$cases)` values of Table 1 of @spanos2024 to
within `r num(spanos_tol, 3)` (within `r num(spanos_tol_r, 3)` with the mean
rounded as in the source), and the two-bound value equalled one minus the p
value of the z-based two one-sided tests [@lakens2017] in all
`r int(r_toster$cases)` random intervals checked with TOSTER. The R and Python
twins agreed in all `r int(r_sevpar$cases)` random cases. The value treats the
standard error as known, so in small samples, it overstates severity. That
standard error must describe the sampling distribution at the bound, which the
standard error at the estimate does not do for a proportion near zero. And the
value is nominal, taking no account of selection, such as a subgroup chosen
after seeing the data. The help now states all three limits and the apps the
first and the last. Both attribute the one-bound value to Mayo and Spanos
[-@mayo2006] and call the two-bound minimum the package's own extension. Whether
the error-statistical explication of severity is the right one is itself
disputed [@vandongen2023], which no document of the package mentions.

## SEM compilation

`compile_sem()` wrote byte-identical lavaan syntax in R and Python for
`r int(r_semparity$cases)` random theories. In `r int(r_sem_id$cases)` random
acyclic theories without bows, every compiled model was locally identified, and
`r int(r_sem_eq$agreements)` of them equalled the theory's model written out in
full. The others contain a measured construct that no proposition names, which
lavaan's defaults then free. Every defined effect equalled the total effect from
the coefficient matrix, in `r int(r_sem_eff$cases)` effects in graphs with
loops. The comment on a bow, a path together with a covariance between the same
two constructs, said that the path is not identified, which was wrong in the
`r int(r_bow$discrepancies)` of `r int(r_bow$cases)` theories that supply an
instrument. It now says that the path may not be identified unless the theory
supplies one. The block of zero covariances states exact zeros, so a small
correlation the theory omits can make the global fit reject a model whose
propositions are all true. That is unchanged.

## The exact simulation and what it does not show

The exact method of `simulate()` agreed with the matrix exponential in all
`r int(r_expm$cases)` random runs. It agreed with ODE solvers, DOP853 in Python
and lsoda in R, in all `r ode_text` whose reference solution stays below
10^12^ in absolute value, and the twins gave bit-identical trajectories in
`r int(r_simpar$cases)` runs. The Euler warning followed its documented rule in
all `r int(r_euler$cases)` runs. Version `r pkg_version` makes the exact method
the default, as the 0.7.0 notes had promised.

The computation is correct, but a run shows less than the propositions might
suggest. The file states no gains or damping, so whether a feedback loop grows
or settles is set by the gain against the damping, both defaults the theory does
not state. An acyclic theory decays for any positive damping. A relation stated
as 'causes' or 'mediates', which gives no sign, is coupled positively, while
'moderates' and 'associates' couple nothing. Over the default time window, a
chain that decays in the long run shows only a rise. The trajectory is one
linear system consistent with the stated signs, among many that the theory
allows. The help and the apps now say so, and the apps name the settings beside
each run.

# The checklist and its score {#sec-checklist}

## What the items read

The checklist has `r nw(n_items)` items, combined in a weighted mean of the
items that apply. Most read whether a field is filled in or how a prediction is
labelled: whether a prediction is typed point, interval or directional, whether
its bounds are finite (not how wide they are), whether every construct has a
definition, a measure and boundary conditions, whether each proposition has a
mechanism (not what it says), whether a rival is named and whether a formal
model of a listed type is declared. The derivation chain and diagnosticity check
content against the graph where the file gives them something to check: the
derivation chain reads each stated claim against the causal graph, and
diagnosticity reads a rival's propositions where it states them. The
non-redundancy screen compares the words of definitions. A declared severity
replaces the rubric's value in one item, and test outcomes reach the score only
through the parsimony item. The help and the dossier now describe the items in
these terms.

## The adversarial and strong demonstrations

```{r}
#| label: demo-numbers
hollow <- "adversarial/hollow.theory.yaml"
xfile <- "adversarial/placeholder-x.theory.yaml"
bs <- "adversarial/blue-socks.theory.yaml"
bsr <- "adversarial/blue-socks-refuted.theory.yaml"
rt3 <- "adversarial/rt3-astrology.theory.yaml"
n_adv_pass <- sum(live$gate[live$set == "adversarial"] == "pass")
n_adv_valid <- sum(live$valid_full[live$set == "adversarial"])
n_adv_moved <- sum(live$score[live$set == "adversarial"] != old$score[live$set == "adversarial"])
enc_moved <- strong_enc[live$score[match(strong_enc, live$file)] !=
                          old$score[match(strong_enc, live$file)]]
s1_enc <- strong_enc[grepl("s1-", strong_enc)]
s3_enc <- strong_enc[grepl("s3-", strong_enc)]
moved_text <- if (n_adv_moved == 0) "No adversarial file moved, so a" else
  paste0(Nw(n_adv_moved), " adversarial files moved. A")
# Why no weighting helps: a file that passes every applicable item scores 100
# under any positive weights, and every strong file has an item below 1.
bound_text <- if (hollow %in% full_adv && strong_below) {
  paste0("No positive weighting of the items can rank a strong theory at or ",
         "above the hollow file, which passes every item that applies to it ",
         "and so scores ", sc(dm(hollow, "score")), " under any weights.")
} else ""
```

The audit built files that should score low if the score measured the quality of
a theory, and encoded theories that should score high. The demonstrations
directory holds them, and the live run of this report scores them with the
package in this repository (@tbl-demos).

::: {.callout-note}
## Live run
The demonstrations below were recomputed when this report was rendered, by
`demonstrations/run.R` with theoryforge `r pkg_version` loaded from
`r/theoryforge` in this repository`r pkg_commit` (source hash `r pkg_hash`),
which read checklist `r checklist_live`. The live run
`r if (live_same) "is identical to" else "differs from"` the stored run in
`data/demonstrations-0.8.0.csv`. The run on f72ce4c read checklist
`r checklist_old`.
:::

The `r nw(n_adv)` adversarial files are a tautological theory whose predictions
are true by definition, a vague one whose constructs cannot be observed, an
astrological theory whose every recorded test failed, a hollow file whose
mechanism reads 'because', a file whose every text field is the letter 'x' and
an implausible theory in which blue socks raise exam marks, as written and with
every test failed. `r cap(all_or(n_adv_valid, n_adv))` of them pass full
validation and `r all_or(n_adv_pass, n_adv)` pass the gate. They score from
`r sc(min(adv_scores))` to `r sc(max(adv_scores))`. The hollow file scores
`r sc(dm(hollow, "score"))` and the 'x' file `r sc(dm(xfile, "score"))`. The
`r nw(length(strong_enc))` strong theories, light deflection, prospect theory,
Hick's law and Michaelis–Menten kinetics, encoded only from their sources, score
from `r sc(min(enc_scores))` to `r sc(max(enc_scores))`, and
`r all_or(n_adv_above_enc, n_adv)` adversarial files outscore every one of them.
Re-encoded with every field the sources allow, they score from
`r sc(min(consc_scores))` to `r sc(max(consc_scores))`, and
`r nw(n_adv_above_consc)` of the `r nw(n_adv)` adversarial files still score
above all of them. Agents who knew the checklist wrote all these files, so they
demonstrate what the score rewards rather than measure how real theories fare.

Apart from the parsimony item, the score does not read the test record. The
blue-socks file scores
`r sc(dm(bs, "score"))` with its tests passed and `r sc(dm(bsr, "score"))` with
every test failed, and the astrological theory, refuted by every recorded test,
scores `r sc(dm(rt3, "score"))`. In the red team's files, flipping or removing
every outcome left score and gate unchanged. A checklist applied before data
need not read outcomes, and the score now says that it describes completeness
and that test outcomes are read only by the parsimony item. But a reader who
sees a high score beside a refuted theory needs that sentence.

Version `r pkg_version` lowered `r nw(length(enc_moved))` of the strong theories
as first encoded, light deflection from `r sc(dm(s1_enc, "score", "old"))` to
`r sc(dm(s1_enc, "score"))` and Hick's law from
`r sc(dm(s3_enc, "score", "old"))` to `r sc(dm(s3_enc, "score"))`, because the
claim-form rubric now rates a point prediction without finite bounds as
directional. `r moved_text` correction that makes the rubric consistent with the
precision item widened the gap in this demonstration in the wrong direction.

## Weight dependence

The report gives each score a range, `aggregate_range`, from equal weights and
from each weight halved or doubled in turn. Version `r pkg_version` describes it
as the extremes of these particular weightings. To see how far the score moves
when the weights change together, this report recomputed the score of each
adversarial and strong file under `r int(n_draw)` weightings in which every
weight was multiplied by its own factor between one half and two, uniform on a
log scale. The choice of distribution is itself a convention, as the second
reader of the red team noted of the audit's own choice. Under it, the draws fell
outside a file's reported range in a median of
`r pct(median(outside[!is.na(width_ratio)]))` of weightings, and the central
`r pct(ci_level)` of draws was a median of
`r num(median(width_ratio, na.rm = TRUE))` times as wide as the reported range.
Every adversarial file outscored every strong theory as first encoded in
`r pct(p_adv_over_enc, 1)` of the weightings, while the tautological file
outscored the most completely re-encoded theory, light deflection, in
`r pct(p_rt1_over_s1c)` of them. The weights thus decide the order of files with
similar scores but hardly change the gap between the adversarial files and the
theories as first encoded. `r bound_text`

## The gate and the derivation chain with loops

```{r}
#| label: loop-numbers
lp <- function(n) paste0("loops/", n, ".theory.yaml")
acyc <- lp("contradicted-acyclic"); thru <- lp("loop-through-claim")
unrel <- lp("unrelated-loop")
gate_phrase <- function(g) ifelse(g == "pass", "passes", paste("is", g))
gate_past <- function(g) ifelse(g == "pass", "passed", paste("was", g))
chain_phrase <- function(s) c(pass = "passes", fail = "fails", warn = "warns")[[s]]
thru_sigma_gate <- tf_check(tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", thru)), cycles = "sigma")$gate
thru_same <- dm(thru, "score") == dm(thru, "score", "old")

# A phenomenon behind a feedback loop, beside a prediction that states no
# claim: what check() and the preregistration say under each reading.
k_list <- function(ids) lapply(ids, function(i) {
  list(id = i, label = i, definition = paste("Construct", i, "as defined here."),
       measurement = list(paste0("m_", i)), boundary_conditions = list("adults"))
})
ph_th <- list(
  schema_version = "1.1", id = "phenomenon-loop", title = "Phenomenon behind a loop",
  maturity = "testing", constructs = k_list(c("a", "b")),
  propositions = list(
    list(id = "p1", from = "a", to = "b", relation = "increases", mechanism = "m."),
    list(id = "p2", from = "b", to = "a", relation = "increases", mechanism = "m.")),
  predictions = list(list(id = "h1", statement = "a raises b", type = "directional",
                          derives_from = list("p1"))),
  phenomena = list(list(id = "ph1", statement = "a lowers b",
                        claim = list(kind = "effect", x = "a", y = "b",
                                     sign = "negative"))))
ph_rep <- function(cy) {
  r <- tf_check(ph_th, cycles = cy)
  dc <- Filter(function(i) i$id == "derivation_chain", r$items)[[1]]
  pr <- strsplit(tf_preregister(ph_th, cycles = cy), "\n")[[1]]
  # The header line on phenomena.
  l <- grep("phenomenon states", pr, value = TRUE)
  stopifnot(length(l) == 1)
  list(gate = r$gate, chain = dc$status,
       named = "ph1" %in% unlist(dc$phenomena_not_checked),
       line = sub(".*: ", "", l))
}
ph_refuse <- ph_rep("refuse")
ph_sigma <- ph_rep("sigma")
phen <- "phenomena/contradicted-phenomenon.theory.yaml"
pred <- "phenomena/contradicted-prediction.theory.yaml"
```

The gate passes unless one of the `r nw(n_blockers)` blocking items fails:
falsifiability, which asks that some prediction be typed as a claim that rules a
result out, and the derivation chain, which asks that every prediction cite
declared propositions whose graph entails any claim it states and that no stated
phenomenon be contradicted. A file marked as a draft makes the gate advisory.
The gate's labels are the author's, so a file can pass on a label. The
philosophy lens showed that a prediction saying that x 'may raise or lower y,
depending on context' passes the falsifiability item and the gate once it is
labelled directional, and a rerun on version `r pkg_version` gives the same.

At f72ce4c, the derivation chain read claims as if the graph had no loops and
counted a claim it could not read as derived. Any feedback loop anywhere in the
propositions therefore made every claim check pass, so that a loop could let a
file through a gate that its claims would block. The loops demonstrations show
what version `r pkg_version` does instead. A contradicted claim in an acyclic
graph scores `r sc(dm(acyc, "score"))`, and the gate `r gate_phrase(dm(acyc, "gate"))`.
With a loop between two constructs unrelated to the claim, the file scored
`r sc(dm(unrel, "score", "old"))` at f72ce4c, and its gate
`r gate_past(dm(unrel, "gate", "old"))`. It now scores `r sc(dm(unrel, "score"))`, and the gate
`r gate_phrase(dm(unrel, "gate"))`, because a claim that names no construct on a
loop or downstream of one is read as on the graph without the loop
(@sec-loops). A claim whose two constructs lie on a loop is still not read
under the default. For the file with such a loop, the derivation chain
`r chain_phrase(dm(thru, "derivation_chain"))` and names the claim but counts it
as derived, so the file scores `r sc(dm(thru, "score"))``r if (thru_same) ", as at f72ce4c," else ""`
and the gate `r gate_phrase(dm(thru, "gate"))`. Reading the graph by
sigma-separation (`check(cycles = "sigma")`) reads such claims, on the
assumption that each loop settles to a unique equilibrium, and the same file's
gate is then `r thru_sigma_gate`. The documents and the apps now say, with the
gate, that under the default a claim behind a loop blocks nothing.

The derivation chain checks agreement with the graph. It does not ask how far a
prediction goes beyond the propositions: a prediction that restates its one
proposition is entailed, and in the communication lens's count, most of the
entailed verdicts in the shipped examples rest on a single proposition. Stating
a checkable claim can only expose an error and cost points, while leaving claims
out costs nothing. A claim behind a loop costs nothing either, since it counts
as derived, so the score does not show whether such a claim was checked. Only
the item's status and its list of unread claims do. The incentive the
measurement lens described, to disclose less, remains.

## Phenomena

At f72ce4c, a phenomenon whose claim the theory's own graph contradicts left
score and gate unchanged, while the same claim stated as a prediction blocked
the gate. Version `r pkg_version` fails the derivation chain for such a
phenomenon whenever its claim is read, so the gate is now
`r dm(phen, "gate")` in both cases. The score still counts only predictions:
`r sc(dm(phen, "score"))` with the contradicted phenomenon and
`r sc(dm(pred, "score"))` with the contradicted prediction. Under the default
reading, the claim of a phenomenon that names a construct on a loop or
downstream of one is not read, like a prediction's. In a constructed theory of
two constructs that raise each other, with a phenomenon claiming that one lowers
the other beside a prediction that states no claim, the derivation chain
`r chain_phrase(ph_refuse$chain)``r if (ph_refuse$named) " and names the phenomenon" else ""`,
the gate `r gate_phrase(ph_refuse$gate)` and the preregistration answers
'`r ph_refuse$line`' to whether the graph contradicts no claim a phenomenon
states. Read by sigma-separation, the item `r chain_phrase(ph_sigma$chain)`, the
gate `r gate_phrase(ph_sigma$gate)` and the answer is '`r ph_sigma$line`'.

# The amendment appraisal {#sec-appraisal}

```{r}
#| label: appraisal-numbers
flip <- "amendments/sign-flip.theory.yaml"
weak <- "amendments/weakened-sign.theory.yaml"
prot <- "amendments/protects-only.theory.yaml"
app_rows <- vd$group == "Amendment appraisal"
# A new version whose graph cannot be built: the sign reversal with one more
# proposition, to a construct the file does not declare.
flip_th <- tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", flip))
flip_prior <- tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", live$prior[live$file == flip]))
undeclared <- flip_th
undeclared$propositions <- c(undeclared$propositions, list(list(
  id = "p_undeclared", from = flip_th$constructs[[1]]$id,
  to = "undeclared_construct", relation = "increases", mechanism = "m.")))
ap_undeclared <- tf_appraise_amendment(undeclared, flip_prior)
undeclared_lost <- if (length(ap_undeclared$content_lost) == 0) "no content listed as lost" else
  paste("content lost", and_list(unlist(ap_undeclared$content_lost)))
undeclared_text <- if (identical(ap_undeclared$verdict, "progressive")) paste0(
  "And when the new version's graph cannot be built, the new rules are skipped. ",
  "Adding to the sign reversal above one proposition to a construct the file ",
  "does not declare turns ", dm(flip, "verdict"), " into progressive, with ",
  undeclared_lost, ".") else paste0(
  "When the graph of either version cannot be built, the two graphs are not ",
  "compared, and the verdict is then never progressive. Adding to the sign ",
  "reversal above one proposition to a construct the file does not declare ",
  "gives ", ap_undeclared$verdict, ", with ", undeclared_lost, ", since the ",
  "comparison that would find the loss is not made.")
# A refuted point prediction without bounds, relabelled directional: whether
# the appraisal counts the relabelling as a weakening.
relabel <- function(type) list(
  schema_version = "1.1", id = "relabel", title = "Relabel", maturity = "testing",
  constructs = k_list(c("c1", "c2")),
  propositions = list(list(id = "p1", from = "c1", to = "c2", relation = "increases",
                           mechanism = "m.")),
  predictions = list(list(id = "h1", statement = "c2 rises with c1.", type = type,
                          derives_from = list("p1"),
                          claim = list(kind = "effect", x = "c1", y = "c2",
                                       sign = "positive"))),
  test_outcomes = list(list(prediction_id = "h1", passed = FALSE)))
ap_relabel <- tf_appraise_amendment(relabel("directional"), relabel("point"))
relabel_weakened <- any(vapply(ap_relabel$revised, function(r) identical(r$change, "weakened"),
                               logical(1)))
```

`appraise_amendment()` compares two versions of a file and calls the amendment
progressive, degenerating or neutral by rules that borrow the terms of
@lakatos1970. At f72ce4c, the rules compared implied independencies and stated
predictions but not the signs the two graphs entail. An amendment that reversed
the proposition behind a corroborated prediction, so that the new graph
contradicts it, was called `r dm(flip, "verdict", "old")`. Version
`r pkg_version` compares the signs as well. The same amendment is now
`r dm(flip, "verdict")`, with the prediction listed as content lost (the prior's
graph entails it and the new graph contradicts it) and the sign of the effect
listed as lost. An amendment that only weakens that sign to unsigned is
`r dm(weak, "verdict")` where it was `r dm(weak, "verdict", "old")`. An
assumption whose independent predictions are all untested is now classed as
pending rather than ad hoc, so a bold amendment is no longer called degenerating
before its prediction has been tested. When the appraisal asks whether a
retained prediction was weakened, a point or interval label without two finite
bounds now ranks as directional, as the claim-form rubric reads it. Relabelling
a refuted point prediction without bounds as directional
`r if (relabel_weakened) "still counts" else "therefore no longer counts"` as
weakening it, and the amendment is `r ap_relabel$verdict`.

Most limits remain. The appraisal reads what the two files declare and cannot
check it. It cannot tell a prediction from an accommodation:
a subgroup re-description of the anomalous data, recorded as a new prediction
that passed, makes an amendment progressive, and so does an old result listed in
the 'protects' field of a trivial new assumption. The live run shows the second
case, `r dm(prot, "verdict")` with `r dm(prot, "protected_only")` reported as
new only through 'protects'. Whether a new prediction counts as new content or
as an articulation of old content depends on whether it states a
machine-readable claim. A single pass counts as corroboration whatever its
estimate, the severity of the test or the number of failed new predictions
beside it. Appraised one version at a time, a prediction made in one version and
corroborated in the next is never credited. The appraisal has no field that
marks which propositions are central to a theory, so it cannot tell a change to
them from a change at the periphery, which in the auditors' reading is the
distinction Lakatos's term 'hard core' draws. `r undeclared_text`

Version `r pkg_version` reports several of these beside the verdict without
letting them decide it: the new predictions that count as new only through
'protects', the refuted new predictions and the lowest post-data severity of the
passes of each corroborated new prediction. The documents now say that the
verdict holds only if what the two files declare is true and that the rules
cannot tell a prediction from an accommodation. Of the `r nw(sum(app_rows))`
verdicts on the appraisal, the status register counts
`r status_phrase(vd$status[app_rows])`. A function that appraises a chain of
versions, fields for the provenance of data and a severity threshold for
corroboration were recommended for a later release, for which no plan is
published. Even those would rest on the author's
declarations, so the most the appraisal can claim is conditional: if the
declarations are true, these rules give this verdict.

# The generated documents and the apps {#sec-outputs}

```{r}
#| label: outputs-numbers
doc_rows <- vd$group == "Documents and framing"
app_vrows <- vd$group == "Apps"
comm_f <- fd$lens == "communication-and-apps"
# What the dossier's preamble says it flags, against the margin it applies,
# whether the dossier says what the gate checks and marks the blocking items,
# and whether the header of a dossier names how feedback loops were read.
tf_ns <- asNamespace("theoryforge")
margin <- get(".tf_DECLARED_MARGIN", envir = tf_ns)
dossier_lines <- strsplit(tf_dossier(tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", hollow))),
                          "\n")[[1]]
# The preamble is the italic paragraph after the header.
preamble <- paste(grep("^_Generated by theoryforge", dossier_lines, value = TRUE),
                  collapse = " ")
stopifnot(nzchar(preamble))
preamble_says_above <- grepl("a declared severity above the rubric", preamble, fixed = TRUE)
preamble_margin <- grepl(paste("more than", num(margin, 1), "above the rubric"), preamble,
                         fixed = TRUE)
gate_lines <- grep("gate|blocker", dossier_lines, ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)
gate_unexplained <- all(grepl("^- (Gate|Blockers failed):", gate_lines))
n_blocker_marks <- sum(grepl("^\\| [a-z_]+ \\(blocker\\) \\|", dossier_lines))
panic_th <- tf_read(tf_example_path("panic-network.theory.yaml"))
panic_doss <- strsplit(tf_dossier(panic_th), "\n")[[1]]
# The dossier's header and that of the preregistration it holds.
loop_line <- unique(sub("^- Feedback loops: ", "",
                        grep("^- Feedback loops:", panic_doss, value = TRUE)))
doc_text <- c(
  if (gate_unexplained) paste0(
    "The dossier prints the gate's result and the number of blockers that ",
    "failed without saying what the gate checks.") else paste0(
    "The dossier's preamble and the HTML report state what the gate checks, and the ",
    "dossier's checklist table marks the ", nw(n_blocker_marks), " blocking items."),
  if (preamble_says_above) paste0(
    "The dossier's preamble says that it flags a declared severity above the ",
    "rubric, but it flags only one more than ", num(margin, 1), " above it.")
  else if (preamble_margin) paste0(
    "The preamble says that the dossier flags a declared severity more than ",
    num(margin, 1), " above the rubric, the margin it applies."),
  if (length(loop_line) >= 1) paste0(
    "The header of the dossier and of the preregistration names the reading of ",
    "feedback loops, for the panic network under the default '", loop_line[1], "'.")
  else "The header of the dossier does not say how feedback loops were read.")
doc_text <- paste(doc_text, collapse = " ")
```

The preregistration, the dossier, the HTML report and the apps present the
package's results to readers, and at f72ce4c, they presented them as
judgements.
The score was an 'aggregate rigour score' out of 100, the app said that the
checklist 'scores twelve facets of rigour', the dossier was called an audit,
'Derivations check: yes' headed preregistrations whose claims had not been read,
and the app coloured an entailed claim green and a rival's contradicted claim
red. The documentation's own scope sentence, that the score indexes how
completely a theory is specified and says nothing about whether it is true, was
accurate but appeared only on the methodology page and in the READMEs.

Version `r pkg_version` calls the number the checklist score wherever it is
shown. It prints the same scope statement beside the score in the help, the
dossier and the HTML report and with the checklist result in the apps, while the
score on the apps' theory card and in their editor carries only the statement's
first and last sentences, as a hover title that a phone does not show. It opens
the dossier with what is author-entered and what is derived and the
preregistration with what it holds and what must be added before registration,
takes the derivation line from the derivation chain read with the document's own
setting for loops, and uses neutral colours for the causal readings, the
rival comparison and the amendment verdict.

`r doc_text` The apps show each
checklist item's criterion below its id, write the score with its one decimal,
say what content an amendment gives up and show a long list as its first
entries with a way to see the rest. Of the `r int(sum(comm_f))` findings of the
communication lens and its second reader, the status register counts
`r status_phrase(fd$status[comm_f])`. The two apps agree with each other and
with the packages. The lens's comparison of their displayed results found a
difference only in the help, which names the language.

Evidence on automated decision aids suggests that text beside a number may not
change how the number is read. In a review of studies of such aids, automation
bias occurred in naive and expert participants and was not prevented by
training or instructions [@parasuraman2010], although a systematic review lists
training, emphasis on users' accountability and the design of the display, such
as where advice appears on the screen, among its reported mitigators
[@goddard2012]. Every grading of a communication finding, the lenses' and their
second readers', judges how likely a misreading is, and none has been measured.
Study 3 of the protocol would measure it.

# Dependence on the encoding {#sec-encoding}

```{r}
#| label: pilot-numbers
cbe <- rd("pilot/checklist_by_encoder.csv")
units <- rd("pilot/units_agreement.csv")
edges <- rd("pilot/edge_agreement.csv")

impl <- rd("pilot/implications_agreement.csv")
dsa <- rd("pilot/derived_sign_agreement.csv")

par <- rd("pilot/parity_r_python.csv")
prer <- rd("pilot/preregistration.csv")
pert <- rd("pilot/perturbations.csv")
summ <- fromJSON(file.path("data", "pilot", "summary.json"))
n_enc <- length(unique(cbe$encoder))
n_th <- length(unique(cbe$theory))

u_all <- units[units$theory == "all", ]
u_k <- as.numeric(sub("/.*", "", u_all$all_three_same_element))
u_n <- as.numeric(sub(".*/", "", u_all$all_three_same_element))
u_ci <- wilson(u_k, u_n)
ed <- edges[edges$level == "directed" & edges$scope == "all", ]
lit <- unlist(impl[, grepl("^J_literal_basis", names(impl))])
reversals <- sum(dsa$sign_reversals)
ok_lists <- ichk[ichk$package == "ok", ]
n_lists <- nrow(ok_lists)
n_confirmed <- sum(ok_lists$n_confirmed)
lin_acyc <- lin[lin$criterion == "refuse", ]
lin_habit <- lin[lin$theory == "health-habit", ]
hyp_cclt <- prer$hypotheses[prer$theory == "collaborative-cognitive-load" &
                              prer$cycles == "refuse"]
habit_yes <- all(prer$derivations_check[prer$theory == "health-habit"] == "yes")
fill <- pert[startsWith(pert$perturbation, "1e"), ]
fill_after <- as.numeric(sub(".*aggregate: [0-9.]+ -> ([0-9.]+).*", "\\1", fill$changes))
icc_old <- icc1(cbe$aggregate, cbe$theory)
pl <- live[live$set == "pilot", ]
pl$theory <- sub("\\.theory\\.yaml$", "", basename(pl$file))
icc_new <- icc1(pl$score, pl$theory)
spread_old <- tapply(cbe$aggregate, cbe$theory, function(x) diff(range(x)))
spread_new <- tapply(pl$score, pl$theory, function(x) diff(range(x)))
theory_means_old <- tapply(cbe$aggregate, cbe$theory, mean)
old_pl <- old[old$set == "pilot", ]
n_invalid_pilot <- sum(old_pl$valid_full & !pl$valid_full)
n_pilot_files <- nrow(pl)
parity_text <- if (summ$parity_total_differences == 0) {
  "with no difference in any output compared"
} else paste("apart from", int(summ$parity_total_differences), "differences")
claims_text <- if (length(unique(claims$in_all_three)) == 1) {
  paste("only", int(claims$in_all_three[1]), "in each case")
} else and_list(int(claims$in_all_three))
reversal_text <- if (reversals == 0) {
  "No derived sign ever reversed between encoders. The"
} else paste(Nw(reversals), "derived signs reversed between encoders, and most")
claims_union <- and_list(paste(int(claims$union), "for", th_lab[claims$theory]))
edges_common <- and_list(paste(int(ed$in_all_three), "of", int(ed$union), "for",
                               th_lab[ed$theory]))
spread_old_text <- and_list(paste(num(spread_old), "points for",
                                  th_lab[names(spread_old)]))
spread_new_text <- and_list(paste(num(spread_new), "points for",
                                  th_lab[names(spread_new)]))
spread_now_text <- if (identical(spread_old_text, spread_new_text)) {
  paste(", as they do at", pkg_version)
} else paste0(", and within ", spread_new_text, " at ", pkg_version)
icc_new_text <- if (identical(num(icc_new, 2), num(icc_old, 2))) {
  paste("and the same at", pkg_version)
} else paste0("and is ", num(icc_new["icc"], 2), " (", num(icc_new["lower"], 2), " to ",
              num(icc_new["upper"], 2), ") at ", pkg_version)
# Sources of the disagreements over the kind of element, as the analyst
# attributed them.
src_tab <- strsplit(strsplit(u_all$disagreements_by_source, "; ")[[1]], "=")
src_n <- setNames(as.numeric(vapply(src_tab, `[`, "", 2)),
                  vapply(src_tab, `[`, "", 1))
stopifnot(setequal(names(src_n), c("encoder", "format", "verbal")),
          sum(src_n) == u_n - u_k)
# A pair of encodings with the same independence model over the constructs all
# three encoders of a theory used (im, from the summary) whose literal basis
# statements differ.
pairs <- c("enc-1/enc-2", "enc-1/enc-3", "enc-2/enc-3")
same_model <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(im)), function(i) {
  j <- unlist(im[i, paste0("J_indep_", pairs)])
  l <- unlist(impl[impl$theory == im$theory[i], paste0("J_literal_basis_", pairs)])
  data.frame(theory = im$theory[i], pair = pairs, j = j, lit = l)
}))
same_model <- same_model[same_model$j == 1, ]
same_text <- if (nrow(same_model) >= 1) {
  s <- same_model[which.min(same_model$lit), ]
  paste0("Two encoders of ", th_lab[s$theory], " had the same independence ",
         "model over their shared constructs and a literal Jaccard index of ",
         num(s$lit, 2), ".")
} else ""
# What filling the form without changing a statement does at this version:
# every empty mechanism restates its relation, every construct takes the
# theory's boundary conditions and a construct without a measure gets 'a
# rating of' its label (perturbation 1e of the pilot).
fill_form <- function(th) {
  bc <- th$boundary_conditions
  th$propositions <- lapply(th$propositions, function(p) {
    if (is.null(p$mechanism) || !nzchar(trimws(paste(p$mechanism, collapse = "")))) {
      p$mechanism <- paste0(p$from, " ", p$relation, " ", p$to, ".")
    }
    p
  })
  th$constructs <- lapply(th$constructs, function(k) {
    k$boundary_conditions <- bc
    if (length(k$measurement) == 0) {
      k$measurement <- list(paste("a rating of", tolower(k$label)))
    }
    k
  })
  th
}
fill_now <- vapply(pl$file, function(f) {
  tf_check(fill_form(tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", f))))$aggregate_score
}, numeric(1))
fill_same <- isTRUE(all.equal(range(fill_now), range(fill_after)))
fill_text <- if (fill_same) {
  paste0(", and the final ", pkg_version, " gives the same range.")
} else paste0(". At ", pkg_version, ", the same filling moves the files to between ",
              sc(min(fill_now)), " and ", sc(max(fill_now)), ".")
```

Every output of the package describes a file, and a verbal theory can be written
into a file in more than one defensible way. The pilot measured how much this
matters with `r nw(n_enc)` encoders and `r nw(n_th)` theories.

The computations on each file were correct. The `r nw(n_pilot_files)` files gave
identical results in R and Python, `r parity_text`. A separation reader written
for the pilot, which does not use theoryforge, confirmed all
`r int(n_confirmed)` implied independencies in the `r int(n_lists)` lists the
package produced, and `r int(sum(lin_acyc$agree))` signs derived on the acyclic
files agreed with sampled linear models, with no exception.

The files differed. Of `r int(u_n)` source statements, `r int(u_k)` became the
same kind of element in every encoder's file (`r pct(u_k / u_n)`,
`r pct(ci_level)` interval from `r num(100 * u_ci[1], 0)` to `r pct(u_ci[2])`),
with Fleiss' kappa `r num(u_all$fleiss_fine, 2)` for the kind of element and
`r num(u_all$fleiss_claim, 2)` for whether a statement carries a claim the
package can check. Of the claims stated by any encoder (`r claims_union`), every
encoder stated `r claims_text`. Of the directed edges any encoder drew, every
encoder drew `r edges_common`. `r reversal_text` disagreements were between
zero and nonzero, or between a fixed and an open sign. From the same text of
collaborative cognitive load theory, the encoders produced
`r and_list(int(hyp_cclt))` preregistered hypotheses, because the format does
not say when a stated relation should also be a prediction. The analyst
attributed the `r int(u_n - u_k)` statements that did not become the same kind
of element to the encoders' conventions (`r int(src_n["encoder"])`), the format
(`r int(src_n["format"])`) and the source text (`r int(src_n["verbal"])`), so
most of that disagreement is of a kind that a written encoding protocol, as in
Study 1 of the protocol, could address. The kappas and the interval above treat
the statements as independent, although they are nested in `r nw(n_th)`
theories and one agent segmented and coded them all.

Literal agreement on the implied independencies, as Jaccard indices between the
basis statements of pairs of encoders, ranged from `r num(min(lit), 2)` to
`r num(max(lit), 2)`. That measure falls whenever encoders use different
constructs or choose different conditioning sets, even when their graphs imply
the same independencies. `r same_text` Over the constructs that all three
encoders of a theory used, the independence models agreed with Fleiss' kappa of
`r and_list(num(two$fleiss_kappa, 2))` for `r and_list(th_lab[two$theory])`,
and all three encoders agreed on `r pcts(two$all_three_agree)` of the
statements compared. For habit, all three agreed on
`r pct(hb$all_three_agree)` of them, but kappa was `r num(hb$fleiss_kappa, 2)`.
One choice the text leaves open, whether habit prompts repetition directly or
through behaviour, decides whether many of the statements are independences:
the share of statements of independence was `r pcts(hb_share, 1)` in the three
encodings. Kappa is unstable when the shares differ this much, and no interval
is given for any of these kappas, since the statements of one theory are not
independent units.

The perturbations, which change one element at a time, traced the disagreements
in the derivations that they examined to ambiguity in the source text, to the
format (an interaction encoded with the 'moderates' relation becomes an unsigned
edge and leaves open a main effect the theory states) or to the package's
conservative reading of signs in loops of more than one cycle, which left open
`r and_list(int(lin_habit$package_open_sampling_one_sign))` signs in the habit
files that every sampled stable linear model fixed.

The checklist scores of the encoders of one theory lay within
`r spread_old_text` at f72ce4c`r spread_now_text`.
That closeness says little about reliability. Most items were
the same in every file because the texts lack what they ask for, numbers,
measures, rivals and formal models, and the spread came almost entirely from
whether an encoder filled in the mechanism field. At f72ce4c, filling the form
without changing any statement of a theory moved every file to between
`r sc(min(fill_after))` and `r sc(max(fill_after))``r fill_text` The share
of the variance of the score that lay between theories, ICC(1), was
`r num(icc_old["icc"], 2)` at f72ce4c, with a `r pct(ci_level)` interval from
`r num(icc_old["lower"], 2)` to `r num(icc_old["upper"], 2)`, `r icc_new_text`.
With `r nw(n_th)` theories, the interval spans almost every possible value, so
the pilot cannot say whether the score separates theories at all. At
`r pkg_version`, `r nw(n_invalid_pilot)` of the files that passed full
validation at f72ce4c no longer do, because their encoders labelled a prediction
directional while its claim states no direction, which the release now refuses.

The pilot's limits are severe. The encoders were agents of one model family that
read the same documentation, the sources were short summaries that one agent
wrote, and one agent matched the constructs. The pilot says nothing about how
far human researchers would agree and gives no standard for whether any encoding
is faithful. It does show that the package's derivations can be trusted as
computations on a file, while the file is one of several defensible encodings,
and that the scores and derivations describe the encoding rather than the
theory. Expert encoding does not remove the problem. When one research group
encoded a large set of behaviour-change theories, every theory could be
represented, but about half of the encodings were changed in their constructs,
their relations or both after feedback from the theories' authors or other
experts [@hale2020].

# What version `r pkg_version` changed {#sec-changes}

```{r}

# The habit files read by sigma-separation: the claims of predictions that the
# graph does not entail, those of them to which the pilot's sampled stable

open_claims <- function(th) {
  Filter(function(c) c$source == "prediction" && c$verdict != "entailed",
         tf_entailments(th, cycles = "sigma")$claims)
}
hab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(habit_files, function(f) {
  enc <- basename(dirname(f))

          lcp$verdict == "package_open_sampling_one_sign")

  })

             refuse_gate = live$gate[live$file == f], open = length(oc),
             one_sign = sum(one), n_mod = sum(mod),
             gate_inc = tf_check(th_inc, cycles = "sigma")$gate,
             open_inc = length(open_claims(th_inc)))
}))
sigma_text <- if (length(unique(hab$gate)) == 1) {
  paste(unique(hab$gate), "for all", nw(nrow(hab)), "habit files")
} else and_list(paste(hab$gate, "for", hab$enc))
refuse_text <- if (all(hab$refuse_gate == "pass")) "passes" else
  and_list(hab$refuse_gate)
both_signs_all <- all(hab$open > hab$one_sign)
moderates_text <- if (both_signs_all) paste(
```
