```{r}
n_files_one <- sum(hab$one_sign > 0)
inc_text <- if (all(hab$n_mod == 1) && all(hab$open_inc == 0) &&

# Table captions that name the version.
cap_status <- paste0("Status in version ", pkg_version, " of every finding and verdict in the register.")
cap_critical <- paste0("The critical findings and their status in version ", pkg_version, ".")
cap_demos <- paste0("Demonstrations at f72ce4c and in the live run of version ", pkg_version, ": score, gate and derivation chain, with 'a → b' where the value changed.")
cap_demos_other <- paste0("Other results of the demonstrations that changed between f72ce4c and the live run of version ", pkg_version, ". An empty list is written 'none'.")
cap_review <- paste0("Problems of the corrected rules and documents that reviews of the release reported, rerun when this report was rendered on version ", pkg_version, ".")

# Problems that the review of the release reported, rerun here. Each row

p_ref <- tf_check(panic_th)
p_sig <- tf_check(panic_th, cycles = "sigma")
p_dc <- Filter(function(i) i$id == "derivation_chain", p_ref$items)[[1]]
holds_word <- function(h) if (h) "Still holds. " else ""
rv <- data.frame(

    "A phenomenon's claim behind a loop was skipped without a warning, and the preregistration said no phenomenon was contradicted",
    "A prediction left unread by a loop lowered the score",

    "Relabelling an unbounded point prediction as directional counted as weakening it",
    "The dossier did not say what the gate checks",
    "The dossier said it flags a declared severity above the rubric",
    "Documents did not say how feedback loops were read"),
  holds = c(

    length(loop_line) == 0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
rv$State <- paste0(vapply(rv$holds, holds_word, character(1)), c(
  paste0("The unrelated-loop file scores ", sc(dm(unrel, "score")), " and its gate is ",
         dm(unrel, "gate"), "."),
  paste0("The derivation chain ", chain_phrase(ph_refuse$chain),
         if (ph_refuse$named) " and names the phenomenon" else "",
         ", the line reads '", ph_refuse$line, "' and the gate ",
         gate_phrase(ph_refuse$gate), "."),
  paste0("The panic network scores ", sc(p_ref$aggregate_score), " under the default and ",
         sc(p_sig$aggregate_score), " by sigma-separation, its derivation chain ",
         c(pass = "passing", warn = "warning", fail = "failing")[[p_dc$status]], " at ",
         num(p_dc$score, 1), " under the default."),
  paste0("The sign reversal with a proposition to an undeclared construct is ",
         ap_undeclared$verdict, "."),
  paste0("The refuted prediction relabelled is ",
         if (relabel_weakened) "weakened" else "not weakened", ", and the amendment is ",
         ap_relabel$verdict, "."),
  if (gate_unexplained) "The dossier prints only the gate's result." else paste0(
    "The preamble states what the gate checks, and the table marks the ",
    nw(n_blocker_marks), " blocking items."),
  if (preamble_margin) paste0("The preamble says more than ", num(margin, 1),
                              " above the rubric, the margin applied.") else
    paste0("The dossier flags only a margin of more than ", num(margin, 1), "."),
  if (length(loop_line) >= 1) paste0("The header reads 'Feedback loops: ", loop_line[1], "'.")
  else "No header line names the reading."))
n_rv_hold <- sum(rv$holds)
rv_text <- paste0(
  "@tbl-review lists the main problems of the corrected rules and documents that ",
  "the reviews reported and that this report reruns when it is rendered. ",
  if (n_rv_hold == 0) paste0("None of the ", nw(nrow(rv)), " holds at this commit.")
  else paste0(Nw(n_rv_hold), " of the ", nw(nrow(rv)), if (n_rv_hold == 1) " holds" else
                " hold", " at this commit, and the register, built from the audit of ",
              "f72ce4c, does not list ", if (n_rv_hold == 1) "it." else "them."))
```

@tbl-status counts the status of every finding and verdict. Of the
`r int(n_find)` findings, `r int(nf("fixed"))` were fixed and
`r int(nf("reported"))` are now reported beside the result. In all,
`r int(nf("reworded"))` were reworded with the behaviour unchanged,
`r int(nf("unchanged"))` are unchanged and `r int(nf("deferred"))` deferred.
For the `r nw(n_crit)` critical findings, the counts are
`r status_phrase(fd$status[crit_f])` (@tbl-critical), and for the
`r int(n_major)` major findings, they are `r status_phrase(fd$status[maj_f])`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-status
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_status
stt <- data.frame(
  Status = cap(status_order),
  Findings = sapply(status_order, function(s) sum(fd$status == s)),
  Verdicts = sapply(status_order, function(s) sum(vd$status == s)))
stt$All <- stt$Findings + stt$Verdicts
stt <- rbind(stt, data.frame(Status = "All", Findings = nrow(fd),
                             Verdicts = nrow(vd), All = nrow(fd) + nrow(vd)))
kab(stt)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-critical

ct$title <- sub("\\.$", "", ct$title)
kab(data.frame(Finding = ct$title, Status = cap(ct$status)))
```

@tbl-demos sets the demonstrations at f72ce4c beside the live run. Where a value
did not change, one value is shown. @tbl-demos-other lists the other changes in
the stored results: the appraisal of the amendments and full validation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demos
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_demos
arrow <- function(a, b) ifelse(a == b, a, paste(a, "→", b))
dt <- data.frame(
  File = short(live$file),
  Score = arrow(sc(old$score), sc(live$score)),
  Gate = arrow(old$gate, live$gate),
  Chain = arrow(old$derivation_chain, live$derivation_chain))
kab(dt)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demos-other
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_demos_other
val <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x) | x == "", "none", x)
other_cols <- c(valid_full = "full validation", verdict = "verdict",
                content_lost = "content lost", entailments_lost = "entailments lost",
                signs_lost = "signs lost", protected_only = "new only through protects")
change_text <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(live)), function(i) {
  parts <- character(0)
  for (cl in names(other_cols)) {
    a <- val(as.character(old[[cl]][i]))
    b <- val(as.character(live[[cl]][i]))
    if (cl == "valid_full") {
      a <- ifelse(a == "TRUE", "passed", "failed")
      b <- ifelse(b == "TRUE", "passed", "failed")
    }
    if (a != b) parts <- c(parts, paste0(cap(other_cols[[cl]]), ": ", a, " → ", b))
  }
  # A lost entailment is written as the claim, its verdict under the prior
  # and its verdict under the new version.
  parts <- gsub("(\\S+) (entailed|contradicted|undetermined) (entailed|contradicted|undetermined)",
                "\\1 (\\2, now \\3)", parts)
  paste(parts, collapse = ". ")
}, character(1))
keep <- nzchar(change_text)
kab(data.frame(File = short(live$file)[keep], Change = change_text[keep]))
```

Some rules were corrected. The amendment appraisal reads signs and lost
entailments, has the pending class and gives no progressive verdict when a
graph cannot be built. A weakening is judged by the regions rather than the
labels, with a point or interval label without bounds ranked as directional.
The derivation chain reads phenomena and, under the default, every claim that
no loop reaches, the preregistration and dossier take their derivation line from
the same reading of loops as their body, the rubric no longer rates a point
label without bounds as precise and the simulation defaults to the exact
method. Some problems are now reported beside the result: the appraisal lists
novelty that rests on 'protects' alone, refuted new predictions and the
severities of the passes behind a progressive verdict, the derivation chain
names the predictions and phenomena whose claims a loop leaves unread, and the
dossier flags a recorded failure whose estimate lies inside its region. Most of
the rest was rewording: every display now calls the number a checklist score
and says what it describes, the help, the documents and the apps describe the
gate by what its blocking items check, and the documents state the assumptions
of the signs, how loops were read, what 'identified' means and what the
simulation does not show.

The score still rates empty, circular and refuted files highly and passes their
gate, as @tbl-demos shows. Apart from the derivation chain and the narrower
rules above, version `r pkg_version` changed what the score is called and what
is said about it, not what it computes. Declared severities still override the
rubric, a rival named without propositions still earns diagnosticity, labels
still decide the falsifiability blocker and disclosing more still costs points.
The appraisal still cannot tell a prediction from an accommodation.

Two of the pilot's findings bear on the new option `check(cycles = "sigma")`,
under which a claim that the graph leaves open fails the derivation chain. When
this report was rendered, the gate under sigma-separation was `r sigma_text`,
while under the default reading, the claims behind their loops are not read and
the gate `r refuse_text`. `r moderates_text`
In `r nw(n_files_one)` of the files, `r nw(sum(hab$one_sign))` further claims
fail although the pilot's sampled stable linear models gave each of them one
sign, because of the conservative reading of signs in loops of more than one
cycle (finding pilot-5). `r inc_text` A user who follows the preregistration's
advice to read loops by sigma-separation thus sees these files blocked, mainly
for a choice of encoding that the register already records.

The changes made in the release were themselves reviewed before this report, by
AI agents who tested the new rules with random, malformed and constructed
inputs, read the documents and apps and checked the packages against the
requirements of CRAN and PyPI. A second round of corrections addressed the
problems they reported, and its change to the reading of loops was checked
against independent oracles (@sec-loops). `r rv_text`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-review
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_review
kab(rv[, c("Problem", "State")], col.names = c("Problem", "At this commit"))
```

# Is automated appraisal of theories feasible? {#sec-feasibility}

The evidence distinguishes deduction, description by fixed rules and appraisal.
Deduction from a stated graph can be computed soundly, and the package computes
it correctly within stated assumptions: what a set of causal propositions
implies about independencies and signs, what an adjustment can identify, which
directions data of a given kind cannot settle. This is deduction in a strict
sense, exact and checkable, and it is useful, because the implications of even a
small graph are easy to get wrong by hand.

A fixed rule can describe a file. It can say how completely a file states what a
checklist asks for, and it can apply declared outcomes consistently, as the
amendment appraisal does. Mechanical combination of information can match or
exceed human judgement. Across studies of human health and behaviour,
mechanical prediction was on average about 10 per cent more accurate than
clinical prediction, and equal or superior to it in a wide range of
circumstances [@grove2000]. Human appraisals are not a perfect standard either,
since independent peer reviews of the same manuscript agree poorly
[@bornmann2010]. The checklist is limited by what its rules read: labels and the
presence of fields, which an author controls and which say nothing about whether
the theory is true. Summary scores of quality have behaved inconsistently in
another field. In a meta-analysis of clinical trials, the conclusion changed
with the quality scale used to pick out the trials of high quality, and the
authors recommended assessing the relevant methodological aspects one by one
[@juni1999].

No part of the package has shown that it can judge a theory's quality, truth or
fruitfulness, or tell a prediction from an accommodation. Precedents for
computed appraisal exist. ECHO, Thagard's connectionist implementation of the
theory of explanatory coherence, computes which of competing hypotheses to
accept from the explanatory relations a user encodes [@thagard1989], and IMEC
implements explanatory coherence as a model that psychologists can run in R
[@maier2024]. @meehl2002 noted that scientists appraising competing theories use
such attributes as aspects of parsimony, the number, qualitative diversity,
novelty and numerical precision of the facts a theory derives, the number of
facts it misderives and its reducibility to other accepted theories, and
proposed that a statistical composite of these attributes could give an
actuarial basis for theory appraisal. The checklist reads the declared form of
some of them but not their record. It counts no derived or misderived fact. Its
parsimony item reads test outcomes only for auxiliary assumptions added for an
anomaly, its precision item reads declared bounds rather than confirmed
precision, and its derivation chain asks whether stated claims follow from the
graph, not how they fared. No rule of the package has been calibrated against
the later fate of theories, which an actuarial basis of the kind Meehl proposed
would need. Eronen and Bringmann [-@eronen2021] give three reasons why good
psychological theories are hard to develop: the scarcity of robust phenomena,
the doubtful validity of constructs and the difficulty of discovering causal
relations between psychological variables. All three arise before a theory is
written into a file, and checking the file does not address them.

So, as far as this evidence goes, automated appraisal of theories is feasible in
a narrow and conditional sense: the package can derive what an encoded theory
implies and describe how completely and consistently it is stated. This evidence
gives no support for automated appraisal in the sense the maintainer doubted.
No part of the package has shown that it can replace a judgement of a theory's
merit, and nothing in the audit suggests that wording or weights would make it
do so.

# What remains unvalidated {#sec-unvalidated}

```{r}
#| label: unvalidated-numbers
noval <- c("measurement-9", "metascience-and-related-tools-3", "pilot-10")
```

No study has measured how reliably different researchers encode the same
theory, whether the checklist and the appraisal agree with experts who judge the
same theories and amendments, or how readers read the outputs. The register's
findings on these (for example `r and_list(noval)`) are all
`r and_list(unique(fd$status[fd$id %in% noval]))`, because no such study has
been run. `protocol.qmd` in this folder describes `r nw(n_studies)`
preregistered studies with human participants that would measure them. Study 1
measures how far
trained coders following a written protocol produce the same file from the same
published theory, at every level the package reads, beside human and agent
baselines. Study 2 compares the checklist and the appraisal with blind expert
ratings and tests whether known groups of corroborated, refuted and
pseudoscientific theories differ as they should. Its criterion, expert
judgement, is itself fallible, and it tests whether the rules reproduce what
experts conclude with the same concepts, not whether the concepts are the right
ones. Study 3 is a randomised reader
study of how often researchers and editors misread the score, the gate, the
dossier and the appraisal in the 0.7.0 and 0.8.0 wording. A later cliometric
study would ask whether the outputs carry information about the later fate of
theories. Until such studies are reported, the outputs other than the deductions
should be read as descriptions of a file.

# Limitations of the audit {#sec-limits}

The audit has limits of its own, and they bear on its findings in both
directions.

All auditors, second readers and encoders were AI agents of one model family,
and so were the drafter of this report and the agents that classified the
status of each finding and verdict in version `r pkg_version`. Their agreement
may reflect shared training rather than independent confirmation, and defects
that all of them would miss are not in the register. Where they judged how a
reader would understand a display, they judged without readers. Only
`r int(n_chk)` of the `r int(nrow(st))` rows of the status register were checked
again after their classification, and the `r int(n_r2)` rows that the second
round of corrections changed rest on reruns by the agent that updated this
report, without a further check, so some rows may still be misclassified.

The audit examined one commit, and the status of `r pkg_version` was
established by rerunning the audit's evidence and reading the files, not by a
new audit. The changes made for the release were reviewed by AI agents in three
parts, the logic of the corrected rules, their communication and the readiness
of the packages for release, and a second round of corrections followed. This
report reruns only the main problems the review reported (@tbl-review). The
minor ones, most of which concern the wording of documents and displays, are
not checked here. The change of that round to how loops are read was checked against
oracles written by AI agents of the same family, on random graphs and on the
audit's theories, and part of those checks ran on a commit before the last
change, which gives the same verdicts (@sec-loops). Neither the review, the
verification nor this report is a full audit of the final code.

The lenses were chosen in advance. Others, such as an audit of security, of
accessibility or of the performance of the apps on large theories, were not part
of this audit.

Several positions were attributed to authors without their texts. The primary
texts of @lakatos1970, of the works of Popper that the register cites and of
Mayo and Spanos [-@mayo2006] could not be read, and the register marks where a
verdict rests on the auditors' reasoning or on secondary sources instead. This
report attributes positions only to sources whose abstracts or texts were read,
and its use of Lakatos's terms in @sec-appraisal is the auditors' reading of
them.

The demonstrations were built to probe what the score rewards. They were written
by agents who knew the checklist, the strong theories were encoded from short
source texts, and they are not a sample of real theories. They show what the
rules allow, not how often it happens.

There was no human comparison. Neither the checklist, nor the appraisal, nor the
encodings were compared with human judgement, so the audit cannot say how far
the package's outputs agree with experts, only that nothing in the package
establishes that they do.
